description: We are iron oxide, a team of five students passionate about space exploration, technology, and innovation. For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are taking on the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. Our goal is to combine NASA's open data, software development, and creative problem-solving to develop an interactive tool that supports future Mars exploration. We aim to turn complex scientific data into practical, accessible solutions through teamwork and innovation.
summary:
MANS (Mars Autonomous Navigation System) is a native 3D mission-planning and simulated navigation application designed to support future human exploration of Mars, where conventional GPS infrastructure is unavailable.

Using real NASA Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter HiRISE elevation models and satellite imagery, MANS reconstructs Martian terrain and enables users to plan routes across Jezero Crater. Its Rust-based A* algorithm compares the shortest traversable route with a lower-risk alternative that penalizes steep slopes and elevation changes.

MANS also features a first-person astronaut navigation simulation and adaptive route replanning. When a user introduces a simulated terrain obstruction, the system recalculates routes from the astronaut's current simulated position while preserving the mission destination.

To evaluate algorithmic correctness, we independently compared A* results against Dijkstra's algorithm using actual HiRISE terrain. All eight reported real-terrain policy comparisons matched the reference optimal costs.

By integrating NASA terrain observations, 3D visualization, route optimization, and dynamic replanning into one workstation, MANS demonstrates a foundation for GPS-independent exploration planning. Future development will investigate camera-based terrain localization and inertial sensor fusion.
details:
1. Problem and Motivation

Future astronauts exploring Mars will face navigation challenges fundamentally different from those on Earth. Mars lacks an operational GPS-like positioning infrastructure, and its surface contains steep terrain, elevation changes, and regions with incomplete observational coverage.

Traditional route visualization alone is insufficient for planning a Marswalk. Exploration planning must account for terrain geometry, route constraints, and unexpected changes during a mission.

We developed MANS (Mars Autonomous Navigation System) to demonstrate how real NASA terrain observations and computational navigation techniques can be integrated into an interactive exploration workstation.

2. NASA Scientific Data Integration

MANS uses Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter HiRISE observations from Jezero Crater, including a stereo-derived Digital Terrain Model (DTM) and an orthorectified satellite image.

The data-processing pipeline uses Python and Rasterio to extract, align, validate, and organize terrain data into nine adjacent tiles.

The resulting terrain covers approximately 1.55 × 1.55 kilometers, with 1,534 × 1,534 unique elevation samples and approximately 1.01-meter grid spacing.

The application also includes a MOLA elevation dataset for broader regional terrain context.

HiRISE elevation measurements provide the geometric foundation for 3D visualization and route calculation. Simulated obstructions and navigation positions are clearly distinguished from observed NASA data.

3. Software Architecture and Development Tools

MANS was developed as a native macOS engineering workstation using:

  • Rust: Core application logic, terrain processing, navigation algorithms, and route optimization.
  • wgpu / Apple Metal: GPU-accelerated 3D terrain and route rendering.
  • egui / eframe: Native interactive application interface.
  • WGSL: GPU shader programming.
  • Python / Rasterio: NASA terrain extraction, geospatial alignment, and dataset preparation.
  • glam: Vector and matrix mathematics.
  • Git / GitHub: Version control and collaborative development.

The software separates terrain data preparation, rendering, terrain interaction, navigation calculations, and astronaut simulation into independent modules.

The rendering system supports tiled terrain loading, multiple levels of detail, camera controls, surface inspection, and terrain-anchored route visualization.

Navigation operates on a full-resolution elevation grid independently of the graphical level of detail.

4. Mathematical Route Optimization

MANS uses a Rust implementation of the A* search algorithm on a terrain graph constructed from measured elevation samples.

For each movement segment, the system calculates three-dimensional surface distance, elevation change, and slope.

Its traversal cost model is:

C = L[1 + ws(θ/12)²] + we|Δh|

where:

  • L represents surface traversal distance.
  • θ represents slope angle in degrees.
  • ws controls the slope penalty.
  • we controls the elevation-change penalty.
  • Δh represents elevation change.

The shortest-route policy minimizes surface distance under the same hard traversal constraints.

The lower-risk policy additionally penalizes steep terrain and elevation changes.

The pathfinding algorithm excludes missing elevation samples, respects configurable maximum-slope limits, and prevents diagonal movement through blocked corners.

These constraints are engineering assumptions rather than certified astronaut mobility limits.

5. Astronaut Navigation Simulation

MANS provides a first-person navigation mode that lets users explore the actual 3D terrain from a simulated astronaut's perspective.

The system tracks a virtual astronaut's position in the terrain coordinate system, samples elevation to maintain ground-following movement, and calculates waypoint bearings, remaining route distance, and route deviation.

The current position is simulated; the application does not claim to obtain real astronaut coordinates from GPS, cameras, or inertial sensors.

6. Adaptive Replanning

A distinctive feature of MANS is its response to changing mission conditions.

Users can introduce simulated terrain obstructions directly onto the 3D map. These obstructions are converted into blocked regions of the navigation grid.

When the route becomes obstructed, MANS can recalculate the shortest and lower-risk routes from the astronaut's current simulated position.

The system retains the original destination and camera orientation, updates the 3D route visualization, and reports changes in remaining travel distance.

This demonstrates a practical transition from static route planning to interactive, situation-aware mission navigation.

7. Independent Algorithm Verification

We developed a test-only Dijkstra reference solver to independently verify the A* route planner.

The reference implementation separately evaluates terrain connectivity, traversal constraints, path costs, and route statistics.

Using the actual nine-tile HiRISE terrain dataset, eight route-policy comparisons across four endpoint pairs matched Dijkstra's optimal costs within the defined numerical tolerance.

The verification covered tile boundaries, terrain constraints, invalid samples, and regional crossings.

Additional automated tests evaluated route geometry, obstruction handling, replanning behavior, and navigation-state preservation.

These results support the mathematical correctness of the implemented discrete route optimizer; they do not establish real-world astronaut safety.

8. Benefits, Limitations, and Future Development

MANS makes complex planetary elevation data more accessible through an interactive tool that connects scientific observations with route planning and navigation simulation.

Its primary contribution is the integration of real NASA terrain, mathematically defined route optimization, independently verified pathfinding, and dynamic mission replanning.

Current limitations include the absence of real astronaut localization sensors, incomplete characterization of surface hazards, limited geographic coverage, and the use of simulated obstructions.

Future research will investigate visual odometry, terrain-relative localization, inertial navigation, sensor fusion, and additional NASA environmental and mineralogical datasets.

MANS is an educational research prototype, not flight-qualified navigation software.
